issues.item: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: 'Risky Behavior' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other selected items describe fear-based reactivity, hypervigilance, sexual trauma triggers, and intrusive/reliving memory phenomena after rape. In that context, prominent risk-taking pulls in the opposite direction of the otherwise avoidance/vigilance-focused presentation and is not supported by appraisals or maladaptive-strategy items. This creates a within-node and cross-node coherence problem.

vignette:
Meena is a 61-year-old agricultural worker who has spent most of her adult life harvesting crops in the Central Valley. The assault happened three years ago, during the autumn harvest, when she had stayed late to finish a row of tomatoes. A man she recognized from a neighboring farm cornered her near the irrigation shed. She remembers the dogs first - two of them, barking wildly from the back of his truck, their barking drowning out her voice. It was the dogs she focused on during the worst of it, because looking at them was easier than looking at him. When it was over, she walked home in silence, washed herself in the outdoor hose, and never told anyone. She was certain her husband would blame her, or worse, that he would see her differently. She had come to believe that what happened was something she simply had to carry alone.

In the weeks that followed, Meena began to notice changes she could not explain. She would be standing in the field, reaching for a ripe tomato, and suddenly her heart would be pounding, her hands shaking, before she had even understood why. Something in her surroundings - the smell of dust and diesel, the particular angle of late afternoon sun, the sound of a dog barking in the distance - could instantly bring the full memory back, and when it came, it did not feel like remembering. It felt like it was happening right now. She would find herself frozen, her body locked in the same helpless stillness she had felt that evening, as though she were back in that moment and could not move or speak.

The connection between what she saw and what her body did became something she could not control. A dog barking in a nearby yard would reach her ears, and before she had time to think, her entire body would be braced for attack - her shoulders tight, her breath shallow, her eyes scanning for an exit. It was not that she decided to be afraid. Her body reacted to danger before she had even had time to think, and by the time her mind caught up, she was already flooded with the feeling of that evening. This was especially true at night. She had difficulty falling asleep because she needed to stay alert; every creak of the house, every distant sound, kept her wired and watchful, and her husband's hand on her shoulder in the dark would make her jerk away with a sharp intake of breath. She reacted with alarm when someone touched her unexpectedly, even when it was him, even when she knew it was coming.

Her marriage became a terrain of careful navigation. Her husband, confused by her withdrawal and her flinching, began to sleep on the couch. Meena told herself this was better - that it was easier this way. Sexual situations or intimacy had become unbearable. Even a glance from him that felt too tender, too expectant, would send her mind spiraling back to the field, and she would find a reason to leave the room. Her memories of the frightening event were like a film that played over and over, and she had no way to stop it. She never knew what would start it. A certain smell, a tone of voice, the weight of the late afternoon heat - anything could be the trigger, and once it started, her body took over.

At work, she began to avoid certain areas of the farm. She would not go near the irrigation shed. She would cross to the opposite end of the field if she saw a dog tied up near a truck. Her foreman noticed and said nothing, but her output slowed, and she was shifted to lighter work - a kindness that also felt like a confirmation that she was diminishing. She had become someone who startled easily, who could not be touched, who lay awake at night listening for threats that never came.

What finally brought Meena to seek help was not her own suffering, but a moment in the grocery store when a small dog on a leash barked at her from across the aisle, and she dropped her basket, staggered backward into a shelf, and found herself on the floor, sobbing, unable to explain to the concerned strangers why she was so afraid. Her daughter, who had driven her home that day, had asked gently, "Amma, what happened to you?" And for the first time, Meena wanted to answer. She is afraid of what will happen if she tells the truth - that her husband might leave, that her family might see her as broken - but she is more afraid of spending the rest of her years on the floor of a grocery store, undone by a dog's bark.
